txt: A small, terrified smile quivers on her face as she takes the handkerchief and wipes away the tears. She looks disoriented.
Her eyes shimmer over yours. "You're a keen observer," she remarks.
Her hands move over the book covers. The tips of her fingers look rough, stained with yellow. It seems like she has spent a lot of time at work, smoking.
She blinks, eyes welling up with tears, as her hands start searching for something from the pockets of her dress.
She blinks. "What-did-you-say?"
She doesn't reply. Her eyes well up with tears, as she struggles to keep it together.
She folds her hands across her chest.
She gives you a short nod and shifts her attention back to books.
She gives you a short nod, before returning to her books.
She just nods, distant and inconsolable. The bed springs rattle beneath her as she begins to shake.
She just nods, still staring into the distance. Some seagulls fly over her head.
She just nods.
She looks up, too anxious to say anything.
She seems to be confused. Your hands are wrapped around her polyester coat. The fabric feels cold, moist from the sea nearby.
She sighs, but you can detect a slight hint of gratitude and relief from her face.
She sighs.
She steps back and returns her attention to books, pretending this hug didn't happen.
She tries to concentrate on books, but her eyes are full of bewilderment.
She turns away from you in an attempt to recover.
She's crying, too heartbroken to notice you standing next to her.
She's still browsing books.
Something changes in her expression. "No, this is something much worse... Is he in a hospital? How bad is it?"

The situation is oddly intimate -- your cheek is pressed against her shoulder, her hand is trapped between your chest. Five seconds pass and their passing seems so unimaginably long. Then she coughs and says again:
The wind brings a strand of hair to her rough face. "I have a strange cop offering to find my stupid husband. What a day..."
The woman before you nods and returns to her reading.
The woman looks baffled by your personal revelation. "You truly are one *strange* cop, aren't you?" she says, slowly shaking her head.
The woman wipes her face with a sleeve and manages to conjure up a small terrified smile. She looks disoriented.
The working class woman doesn't say anything, her eyes still fixed on something invisible in the distance. Some seagulls fly over her head.
You step in and close your arms around this foreign body, wandering astray in touch. There's a small movement beneath your hands, as you shut your eyes. Then a tiny voice breaks out and asks:

"A 'killer' party? What is it with you and *pulp* staples? My god. Please, no more talk about my daughters. They are fine!" She picks up a book and tries to concentrate. A flock of seabirds passes by.
"A brain condition?"
"A hug monster? How do these two go hand-in-hand?" She hasn't let go of your embrace yet.
"Alright, I'll call the RCM then," she nods to herself.
"Alright, I'll call them..." She breathes in again, trying to steady herself.
"Alright, go ahead. Do you have any questions?"
"And I specifically added that I didn't *need* to know where he was."
"And who should I contact...?"
"And you just... found him there? Lying in the cold?" She shakes her head.
"Annette's a sweet sprout, but she doesn't know anything about marriage. Why am I even talking about this..."
"Are you a police man or a nanny?" She's definitely disturbed by now.
"As I already told you, he has a problem with drinking. And so he... disappears every now and then."
"Because we talked about this. We talked about not wandering off again!" She scoffs. "I don't know what to do! I honestly don't know what to do with his addiction... It just makes me feel weak."
"Can I give you some friendly advice, mister policeman? Don't listen to kids."
"Do *police men* just go around repeating what some kid off the street said?"
"Do what?"
"Even if I had, it wouldn't be missing."
"Excuse me, a *bad husband?*" Her back straightens. "What do you mean?"
"Excuse me, what?" She blinks. "What-did-you-say?"
"Excuse me?!" She blinks. "I don't follow."
"Excuse me?"
"Expired?" She narrows her eyes. "Like a *milk carton*?"
"Fighting for it how?" She hasn't let go of your embrace yet.
"From the kiosk? There's one near the harbour, it's a Frittte. You can look it up."
"God damn it, I already told you -- my husband isn't missing!" She crosses her arms.
"God, should I call them? Should I tell them to come home?"
"Good, that's probably the right thing, thank you..." She nods, but with a wretched expression.
"Good." She lets go of your hug.
"Great." She turns her attention back to the bookstand.
"He's probably in the Pox, drinking with his friends. I sent him to the library a few days ago, but I guess something came up..." She smiles sourly.
"He... has a problem with drinking. And so he... disappears every now and then."
"Hello, I'm Billie. Would you like something to drink? Tea, lemonade?" she asks nervously. "We're out of coffee, I was supposed to get some tomorrow..."
"Hello, detective."
"Hello." She nods, her attention fully focused on reading.
"His old leather jacket."
"Hmh?" She adjusts her scarf, cheeks rough and ruddy from the wind.
"Hmm-hmm-hmm..." She's still browsing books.
"Hmm-hmm-hmm..." She's still mumbling to herself, now reading another paperback.
"Hmm-hmm-hmm..." She's still searching for a book, her eyes wandering over the colourful grid of softcovers.
"Hmm-hmm-hmm." You see a sturdy woman humming to herself. She seems to be browsing books.
"Honestly, not that different from you." She eyes you from head to toe.
"How have I been?" she shakes her head. "You're not here to discuss *me* -- what is this about, officer?"
"How long had he *been* there?"
"How long had he been there?"
"I already told you -- I don't have any. Go bother someone else."
"I can't give you what I don't have." She turns away from you, focusing on the books again.
"I can't..." She covers her mouth. "I can't believe he's still *there*, this is *madness*."
"I did and he is." She takes a step back. "He's also an alcoholic."
"I don't even have a cockatoo. And guess what?"
"I don't know, at home now? Out drinking with his friends? Working?"
"I don't know, the most talkative one?" She's ready to put that question aside.
"I don't mean to disrespect, sir, but *you* are being a bit of a cockatoo here."
"I don't think I introduced myself properly -- I'm Billie. Would you like something to drink?" She looks around the kitchen. "Tea, lemonade? We're out of coffee..."
"I even tried throwing it away once, but he just dug it out of the bin. Can you believe it?" She looks back at you, shaking her head.
"I guess it's better than nothing. Keep fighting on, my fellow comrade." Then she breaks up the hug, her cheeks flushed.
"I guess what I want to know is... how did he die?"
"I haven't seen him for... Well, to hell with him!" She has completely forgotten about her books, staring blank into the distance instead.
"I know you are."
"I really should get this. For myself."
"I see. Well, thank you for... telling me." She rubs her face, runs her fingers over cheeks that have become numb.
"I see..." She withdraws, trying to picture the scene. "And you just... found him there? Lying in the cold?"
"I think it was Thibault's 'The Glinting Curve'." She tucks a strand of hair behind her ear. "It was pretty good..."
"I think, yes. If that's the one on Meroe."
"I will. Of course, officer. As I said, it's probably nothing." The woman takes the slip of paper. It's a phone number.
"I'll take it from here. Thank you." She points at the front door, breathing fast now. Holding herself back.
"I'm alright, you can leave now..."
"I'm not sure about the rest, but softly round sounds about right. He's not in great shape." She stops to think.
"I'm sorry, I don't really understand what you're talking about." She lets go of your hug.
"I'm sorry, I just need a... I don't know what to say." She rests her hand on her forehead, eyes pale like pearls in seawater.
"Is she now?" She dries her hands in the apron underneath her coat. Her eyes narrow.
"Is there anything else I can help you with?"
"Is this about Victor, my husband? Is he in some kind of trouble again? I can come pick him up in the station if that's what..." She stops, her eyes trying to read answers from your face.
"It is."
"It must be true, if it's in a book."
"It shouldn't be long from now. He's never gone for more than a few days."
"It's his *cool jacket*. God knows it's too cold to run around in this, but he refuses to change."
"It's me, Victor, and the kids here," she nods. "We have two daughters, Jennie and Jolie."
"It's not like yours look much better," she says while eyeing yours.
"It's okay. We all feel out of sorts at times." She starts patting your back. "There you go, officer."
"It's you from the bookstand... Did you come to bring my cockatoo back?" She smiles nervously, before the smile vanishes from her face.
"It's you from the bookstand..." She just looks at you for a moment without knowing what to do.
"It's you. From the bookstand." For a moment she seems paralysed, just looking at you. Then she forces herself out of it.
"Jolie is sixteen and Jennie is turning eighteen next month."
"Just tell me, what do I need to do next? Where is he? Can I see him?"
"Just tell me, what happened to Victor?" She looks first at the lieutenant, then back at you.
"Just to return a book of mine, why?" She looks at you quizzically. "Why all those questions, detective? Did he..."
"Khm, officer." A coarse female voice pulls you out of your reverie. "What are you doing?" A swash of water hits the coast behind her figure.
"Looking for something to read." She reverts her attention to a worn out paperback.
"Me?" She looks up briefly. "No one, I'm just a working class woman."
"Mhm, I see. Thanks." She tries to read again.
"Mhm. You're welcome." She reverts her attention back to the book stand.
"Mhm." She reverts her attention to the soggy books on the book stand.
"Mhmh, they came home later. They're good girls."
"Mhmh. Exactly. Go ask for an investment." Her words are clipped, but not unamused. Her eyes turn back to the book stand.
"Mhmh." She returns to her book.
"Money?" She looks up to you, a confused smile crossing her lips. "Does the working class ever have any money?"
"My handkerchief..." She tries to smile through the tears, as she rubs her face with hands like a child.
"My husband? No, he's not."
"My youngest girl, Jolie, is just shy of sixteen. Jennie, she is turning eighteen next month. But we shouldn't even be talking about them!"
"No! No-no-no. I'm not missing my money. End of story." She returns her attention back to the book stand.
"No, I don't. I have a good husband, the kind and helpful sort. And he's *not* missing."
"No, I don't."
"No, I meant -- where is *his body*?!"
"No, I'll call you if something comes up, I'm still..." She rubs her face, runs her fingers over cheeks that have become numb.
"No, I'll do it myself, I just..." She breathes again, holding on to her left side like she's in pain.
"No, I'm Billie." She narrows her eyes. "Is this about my husband, Victor? I can come pick him up in the station if that's what..." She stops, her eyes trying to read answers from your face.
"No, I'm not lying. Why should I lie?" A pause. "Please go to the Frittte kiosk."
"No, he's not. Or maybe he is, I don't know. He's probably in the park, or in Jamrock somewhere. Drinking with his *friends*." She looks away.
"No, no!" Her eyes widen at your misunderstanding. "He is definitely not a cop. I meant that he's a little chubby, that's all."
"No, no..." She breathes in. "I just need to tell my girls..." The air gets sucked out of her lungs suddenly.
"No, no..." she backs off, "my relationship with disco remains irrefutably healthy."
"No, sorry," she puts her hands into her coat pockets, as if cold from wind. "I don't have anything to spare."
"No, well..." She stops. "The lining is hand-sewn. It's blue; I tried to make the thing more weatherproof since he's running around with it in the middle of winter."
"No, you don't." She puts her hands into her coat pockets.

"No, you're not. Don't think that way..." she says, slowly shaking her head. The wind brings a strand of hair to her rough face. "You're just a regular talkative cockatoo and let's leave it at that, okay?"

"No, you're not. Don't think that..." she says, slowly shaking her head. The wind brings a strand of hair to her rough face. "You're the cockatoo who offered to find my stupid husband. Let's leave it at that."
"No. Absolutely not." Her words come out quick as gunshots.
"No. I guess I'll find out when he decides to come back home." She looks at the front door.
"No. I'll call you if something comes up, I'm still a bit..." She rubs her face, blotchy and numb.
"No." She looks you straight into the eye. Her right foot is tapping nervously.
"No." She stops.
"Not all the time. Right now I'm browsing books." She pauses. "Even a working class woman needs something to read."
"Not sure about this one..."
"Nothing. Go read up on them if you're so interested. There's a great book in the bookstore."
"Of course he's not. It's not like he's a pocket watch. I wouldn't just lose him."
"Oh my..."
"Oh, it's in Jamrock. The one at Meroe street. I don't know the official name."
"Oh, no! That's not what I meant!" She takes a step back.
"Oh, thank god, no!" She nearly begins to laugh. "It hasn't come down to *this* yet."
"Oh," she says again, "But he was just..." She looks at the kitchen table, where two cigarette butts are still in the tray.
"Oh... it's a prequel?"
"Oh..." There's a strange sensation as the woman strengthens her grip -- she's hugging you back.
"Oh." She touches her neck, eyes pale like pearls in seawater.
"Oh."
"People gotta eat." She rubs her hands together, anxious. "What is this about? Why are you suddenly asking me about my cooking?"
"Please just leave..."
"Please, let's do."
"Police? I don't follow." She narrows her eyes, trying to understand.
"Report what? He's just out, drinking with his friends... I'm sure the police has better things to do than to chase down local goofballs."
"Right, 'cause working class women come with alcoholic husbands." She glances over your shoulder towards the drunk. "You know what?"
"Right, uh..." She pats you on your back, before gently letting go.
"Right. What about him?" Her face becomes anxious again.
"Say what?" She looks frightened.
"So melodramatic. Victor would hate it."
"So you *are* going to look for him?"
"Some things *are* officer." She nods. Her cheeks are red from the cold.
"Sorry, I'm rambling..." She shakes her head and tries to laugh it off. "It's just that Victor often gets into all kinds of trouble. So, how can I help you?"
"Sorry, officer?" She stares at you in disbelief.
"Thank you for telling, me officer..." She looks down.
"Thank you!" You sense gratitude in her voice. "Please, do... Even though I'm sure he will return home by himself. I'm still sure of that."
"Thank you." She looks down. "Thank you for telling me. I'll call, if..." She runs out of breath.
"That's one way to put it, yes. No offence. I'd also add that he's a little bit chubby."
"The girls are staying at their friend's place tonight, and Victor is... out."
"The what now?!"
"There is no *investigation* here, I can tell you that!" She picks up a book and tries to concentrate. A flock of seabirds passes by.
"They're almost grown up now anyway. They're past the age they need me protecting them from everything now."
"They're not missing, sir."
"Think I read this one already."
"Uh... what are you doing, officer?"
"Um, it's just your average brown leather jacket. But he bought it as a teenager, so..."
"Very well, then. Where is he?" She's getting impatient, her hands now picking on a random book cover.
"Wait... is this where he fakes his own death?"
"Was he drunk?"
"Well, he's... slightly chubby."
"Well, what can you do... I hope that at least that extra lining helps him keep warm at night. I wouldn't like him to catch cold."
"What I was trying to say before is that he's a little bit chubby, that's all. I didn't mean anything offensive!"
"What does anything I said have to do with police? Or is *Police* some kind of disco phenomenon as well?"
"What else... He was wearing a dark brown leather jacket with a bright blue inner lining. The lining is hand-sewn, I made it myself." She sighs, her voice slightly quivering when she adds:
"What happened to him? Tell me." Her neck and cheeks are covered with red blotches, her double chin is shaking.
"What happened to him?" She turns to you. Her neck and cheeks are covered with red blotches, her double chin is shaking.
"What is happening?"
"What kind of questions?"
"What problem?"
"What with?" She tries hard to focus on the book stand.
"What? That's just -- my daughters are perfectly *fine*. They're with their friends down in Jamrock! There's *nothing* to worry about."
"What?" She stares at you with hazy eyes.
"What?"
"Where? Did he run *away*?"
"Who said anything about shame? Stop talking down to me." She puts her foot down. "My husband is not missing."
"Why are we still talking about this? I haven't lost my husband."
"Why do you need to know this? Haven't I repeatedly told you that they are not missing? That they're in Jamrock, safe and well, at some stupid party."
"Why do you think that I smoke?" She looks up, slightly startled.
"Why, do you have any news?"
"Why, it's *that bad*?"
"Wonder if I could bring some of my old books here?"
"Wonderful. The store is open."
"Wonderful."
"Yes, I..." She chokes on something, clutching on to her neck.
"Yes, a sci-fi," she says without reverting her attention from the book.
"Yes, but..." She looks around and takes a deep breath, a little annoyed. "I don't really need to know where my husband is. Not all the time."
"Yes, hello." She nods, her attention fully focused on reading.
"Yes, thank you." She smiles a small, terrified smile, then wipes away her tears. She looks disoriented.
"Yes," she says sharply, "that's what happened to Victor too."
"Yes. Right." A wave of despair sweeps over her face. "He wasn't missing anyway," she tries to say while struggling to maintain a courageous front, "I'm sure he'll be home."
"Yes..." She stops. "The lining is hand-sewn. It's blue; I tried to make the thing more weatherproof since he's running around with it in the middle of winter."
"Yes." She becomes unsettled as she says that, her forehead scrunching up into a worried expression.
"Yesterday morning. He went to the library." Her eyes become cold with recollection. "He went to retrieve my book and he promised, he *promised* he'd walk straight back home."
"You both share *what*?" She doesn't understand.
"You had the strangest what?" She hasn't let go of your embrace.
"You haven't even taken him away?!" There's alarm in her voice.
"You were right. I do have an alcoholic husband. Although not that one."
"You're right, we do smoke worse than chimneys here."
